text.p: The dollar closed slightly lower in Europe as mark short-covering took its toll on some of the recent star performers, traders said.
The short-covering spree hit the lira and sterling, spilling over into other crosses and also dragged the dollar lower. Buying on dips buoyed the dollar in the mid-1.53 mark area.
Dollar sentiment remained bullish and the drift lower was seen as consolidation rather than a change of track.
"It is really a matter of time before we get into really interesting territory and the dollar starts to square up for a test of 1.55 marks and 113 yen," said Bear Stearn's David Brown.
At 1615 GMT the dollar stood at 1.5375/80, down from 1.5395/5405 in late European trading on Tuesday. Against the yen, it stood 112.20/25, little changed from 112.25/30.
The dollar recovered off its low at 1.5348 marks after a senior aide to Russian security chief Alexander Lebed dismissed allegations that Lebed was plotting to use force to seize power, traders said.

The comments were made in response to allegations by Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikow, Lebed's rival, that the security chief was planning to move ahead instead of waiting for the next presidential poll.

The mark's rebound took centrestage after Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said Italy and Spain were likely to join EMU by 2002 but not by 1999, the proposed starting date for the single currency.

With high-yielding European bond markets already in retreat from their recent heady highs, Koebnick's comments helped to accelerate the downmove, which spilled over into the currency market, traders said.
Another Bundesbanker, Reimut Jochimsen, said earlier he saw a threat of social unrest from governments' EMU integration efforts in France but also in other European countries.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he was unable to say if there was room to lower interest rates in Germany.
"All in all, it's been a good day to take profits, covers some mark shorts," said a trader at a UK bank.
U.S. CPI data for September held no surprises for the market. The consumer price index rose 0.3 percent, in line with market expectations.
"The U.S. inflation enviroment remains well behaved and the biggest threat to the dollar is if the economy starts to overheat," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
"The latest inflation figures, including the CPI data, don't suggest the economy is overheating and as a result US assets still remain favourable, and the dollar still looks attractive," Lyons said.
The immediate focus for the dollar will be U.S. capacity utilisation and industrial production data for September, due for release at 1315 GMT on Thursday.
U.S. trade data for August, to be released on Friday, will be more closely eyed, since the gaping trade gap is one of the main fundamental bugbears for the dollar, analysts said.
